Theme

cot noun

a baby’s bed

also crib, baby’s cot

classical

Cic. Sen. 83
Plaut. Truc. 5.13, as cited by Lewis & Short

cūnae, cūnārum f. pl.

noun, first declension, plural

a baby’s bed; cradle

Latin has no separate word for a cot: cūnae, the baby’s bed, from the root of ‘to lie’ (de Vaan 153), serves for both. For an older child’s own bed, lectulus.

Other words

  • lectulus, lectulī m. — little bed; one’s own bed

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Cic. Cat. 1.9: in meō lectulō; Traupman 122: bed (small), lectulus

    Levi–Bini’s lecticulus (p. 37, s.v. lettino) is not in Lewis & Short, which has only lectīcula, a small litter. With bars, lectulus clāthrātus (clāthrō, to set with bars: Cato Agr. 4; Plaut. Mil. 2.4.26, Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • et sī quis deus mihi largiātur, ut ex hāc aetāte repuerāscam et in cūnīs vāgiam, valdē recūsem

    and if some god were to grant that I should turn child again at my age and cry in the cradle, I should firmly refuseCic. Sen. 83

  • lectulus clāthrātus

    a little bed with barscomposed

See also cradle, bed, baby.

SourcesLewis & Short: cunae · Lewis & Short: lectulus · Lewis & Short: lecticula · Lewis & Short: clathro

Michiel de Vaan, Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the other Italic Languages (2008), p. 153, s.v. cūnae. Enrico Levi and Arturo Bini, Il latino come lingua viva (1937), p. 37, s.v. lettino. Traupman and Morgan–Owens have no word for a cot (Morgan–Owens’s cot is the camp bed).

Cicero (Sen.) from the Latinitas loci collections.
